title: The Prior Knowledge Paradox: What to Do with What They Know
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: Despite Ausubel's famous principle that prior knowledge is the most important factor in learning, recent research complicates this assumption. A meta-analysis found prior knowledge shows near-zero correlation with learning gains, and an RCT found background knowledge did not improve learning of new domain material. The critical issue lies in varying definitions, mediators, and moderators affecting how prior knowledge influences learning. Ausubel's advance organisers scaffold and constrain prior knowledge before new instruction, making them more effective than relying on existing familiarity.
points: Prior knowledge correlates near zero with learning gains across studies, contradicting the common assumption that familiarity aids new learning.
The relationship between prior knowledge and learning is mediated by sixteen mechanisms and moderated by learner, knowledge, task, and instructional characteristics.
Advance organisers effectively shape and constrain prior knowledge before introducing new material, outperforming approaches that assume existing familiarity will suffice.
Prior knowledge is defined inconsistently across research, ranging from procedural to conceptual knowledge and misconceptions, preventing valid comparisons and explaining inconsistent findings.
Students felt within-domain material was easier but learned it no better, indicating that reduced mental effort does not guarantee stronger learning gains.
quotes: The most important single factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows. Ascertain this and teach him accordingly.
Of the studies that did measure learning gains, the correlation between higher prior knowledge and learning gains was near 0.
Across every measure of new learning, participants did no better on the new topic in the domain they'd been trained in than on topics from the completely untrained domain.
There are mediators and moderators that run interference, and these ultimately explain whether and how prior knowledge helps, hinders or doesn't do very much at all.
To be useful, knowledge must be relevant, available/activated and organised.
An advance organiser is a tool that provides the learner with a temporary, high-level schema through which the new material can make sense.
Shape, constrain and direct prior knowledge as much as possible before introducing new ideas.” Archived from Cognitive Coaching on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
